title: Homelessness plan funding split and Victoria Street purchase
subtitle: Council approved a Kitchener property purchase with debenture financing and reduced fee-for-service cuts to 10 per cent.
overview: Regional Council met in a special session to decide how to spend $10.2 million in new money for the Plan to End Chronic Homelessness. Council defeated the earlier proposal to spread the money in equal proportion across all requests {{vote:m2}}. It then approved an alternative that cuts fee-for-service requests by 10% instead of nearly 30%, and gives the rest to the original plan requests {{vote:m4}}.

This matters to residents because the fee-for-service organizations deliver front-line services. Delegates and councillors heard that a smaller cut would let those groups keep running their programs. The remaining funds go to the plan's original requests, and staff may direct the extra amount to items such as rent supplements.

Council also approved a recommendation from the January 24 closed session to buy 70-84 Victoria Street North in Kitchener for $19,750,000. It added money to the 2024 capital program and approved debenture financing {{vote:m1}}.

decisions.detail: Council approved acquiring the Kitchener property for $19,750,000 through an assignment of the purchase agreement, added $20,684,000 to the 2024 Facilities Management capital program, and approved debenture authority of the same amount for up to 20 years.
Council defeated the deferred motion to spread the new investment proportionally across all plan and fee-for-service requests, clearing the way for an alternative.
Council waived the notice requirement so the alternative homelessness funding motion could be considered at this meeting.
Council reduced fee-for-service requests by 10% from $3.1 million to $2.79 million and directed the remaining $7.42 million to the original Plan to End Chronic Homelessness requests.

debate: Several councillors were concerned that the earlier approach would cut fee-for-service groups by almost 30%, after Council had approved set amounts based on the budgets those groups presented. They said those groups could not run their programs with such a cut but could manage with 10%.

Support for rent supplements was strong. Councillors said they were told rent supplements help the most people, and one suggested the capital reserve contribution would be the area least affected this year if staff reallocate funds.

Councillors asked whether new federal funding changes the picture. Staff said the federal government has signalled extra money to offset a Reaching Home reduction, but nothing is available yet that would change the staff recommendation. Staff would report back once there is clarity.

A councillor asked whether rent supplement money always goes to landlords. Staff said the Region's own funds go through partners directly to landlords with no exceptions, though other provincial and federal programs may pay tenants directly.

There was procedural discussion. Council had seen the report several times, so it voted down the deferred motion to allow the alternative, and one councillor asked that the alternative be explained to the public before the vote.
